summary: A cross-class romance between Rose and Jack aboard the doomed liner, opposed by her jealous fiance and ended by the freezing sea, remembered by Rose for a lifetime.

hunger.why: A first-class dinner and the steerage party feature food and drink, but no one seeks or lacks it.

thirst.why: No character seeks or lacks water.

feeling-cold-hot.why: The freezing North Atlantic kills Jack and hundreds of others; hypothermia dominates the final act.

sleepiness.why: Jack and Rose cling to the debris exhausted, and old Rose drifts to sleep at the end.

curiosity.why: Rose discovers steerage and the bow, Brock Lovett's submersibles explore the wreck.

explanation-seeking.why: Lovett hunts for the Heart of the Ocean, and old Rose's story answers what happened to it.

skill-acquisition.why: Jack teaches Rose to spit and dance, and she learns to live free; Jack's drawing is a practiced skill.

play.why: The steerage dance, spitting contest, flying at the bow, and Jack's teasing are playful joys.

resource-accumulation.why: The Heart of the Ocean, Cal's fortune, Rose's mother's need to marry money, and Lovett's treasure hunt make wealth a thread.

resource-foraging.why: Lovett searches the wreck for the diamond, and passengers scramble for lifeboats and floating debris.

mental-time-travel.why: Old Rose's memory frames the film, young Rose dreads her planned future, and the couple plot escape from Cal.

fear-of-predators.why: No animal or monster threatens anyone.

fear-of-aggressors.why: Cal shoots at Jack and Rose through the flooding ship, and Lovejoy pursues them.

fear-of-heights.why: Rose hangs from the stern railing, people fall from the rising stern, and the ship tilts to vertical.

disgust.why: Frozen corpses float in the water, briefly.

pain-aversion.why: Drowning, freezing, crushing, and falls kill passengers during the sinking.

pride.why: Jack shouts that he is king of the world, Ismay boasts of the ship, and Rose takes pride in her defiance.

shame.why: Rose's mother dreads the shame of lost fortune, and Cal is humiliated by Rose's choice.

moral-pride.why: Rose stands by Jack against her class, the band plays on, and Andrews and the captain go down with the ship.

guilt.why: Rose's survivor's guilt, Ismay's shame in the lifeboat, and Murdoch's suicide show remorse.

warmth.why: Jack's generosity to Rose and Molly Brown's kindness to Jack warm the cold world of first class.

moral-blame.why: Cal is condemned for cruelty, Molly Brown blames the lifeboat passengers' cowardice, and Rose rejects her class's hypocrisy.

moral-praise.why: Jack's sacrifice, the musicians, and Molly Brown are honored as good.

revenge.why: Cal frames Jack for theft and tries to shoot him out of spite.

compassion.why: Jack saves Rose from the railing and keeps her alive on the debris, and crew and passengers help the helpless.

affiliation.why: Rose joins the steerage party and Jack's circle, and Jack and Fabrizio befriend strangers aboard.

friendship.why: Jack's friendship with Fabrizio and Tommy, and Molly's support, matter in the background.

sadness.why: Jack's death, the mass drowning, and old Rose's lifelong grief give the film its sorrow.

humor.why: Jack's charm at dinner, Molly Brown's wit, and the spitting lesson lighten the romance.

embarrassment.why: Jack in a borrowed tuxedo among the rich, and Rose's mother's disdain, create social awkwardness.

reasoning.why: Rose spars with Cal and the dinner party, and Jack defends his way of life.

coalitional-affiliation.why: First class and steerage are rival worlds, and Rose crosses the line.

status-seeking.why: Cal's arrogance, Rose's mother's social survival, Ismay's speed record, and class rank drive the conflict.

envy.why: Rose's mother covets Cal's fortune, and Cal resents Jack's hold on Rose.

anger.why: Cal's rage at Rose and Jack, and Rose's anger at her mother, boil over.

hatred.why: Cal loathes Jack and would see him dead.

romantic-affiliation.why: Jack and Rose's love story is the whole film.

sexual-attraction.why: The nude drawing and the lovemaking in the car make desire central.

long-term-love.why: Rose keeps Jack in her heart for the rest of her life, as the ending shows.

desire.why: Jack's Paris sketches of a one-legged prostitute hint at a freer life, faintly.

romantic-jealousy.why: Cal's jealousy of Jack drives the villainy, from the framing to the gunfire.

sexual-jealousy.why: Cal finds the nude drawing and learns Rose has been with Jack.

sexual-disgust.why: Cal's possessive treatment of Rose and the forced engagement carry a hint of coercion.

parental-care.why: Steerage mothers hold their children as the ship sinks, and Rose's mother pushes her into the lifeboat.

parental-investment.why: Rose's mother arranges her marriage to secure the family's future.

familial-love.why: Rose's strained bond with her mother and old Rose with her granddaughter frame the romance.
